sections.heading: High-efficiency MOSFET bridge rectifier for AlN MEMS cantilever vibration energy harvester
sections.text:
Ryohei Takei1\*, Hironao Okada1, Daiji Noda2, Ryo Ohta2, Toshihiro Takeshita1, Toshihiro Itoh3, and Takeishi Kobayashi1

1National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-8564, Japan   
2Micronano Open Innovation Center, Micromachine Center, Chiyoda, Tokyo 101-0026, Japan   
3Graduate School of Frontier Sciences, University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, Chiba 227-8563, Japan

\*E-mail: r.takei@aist.go.jp

Received October 12, 2016; revised December 20, 2016; accepted December 28, 2016; published online March 6, 2017

We developed a high-efficiency MOSFET bridge rectifier for use in an aluminum nitride (AlN) piezoelectric MEMS cantilever vibration energy harvester (VEH). The bridge rectifier consists of four MOSFETs with a circuit configuration similar to that of a typical diode bridge rectifier. The output voltage of the full-wave rectification via the MOSFET bridge was simulated with an equivalent circuit model of the AlN VEH, which is extracted from an experimental result. The channel width of the MOSFET was designed to be adopted for use with a high-voltage and low-current AlN VEH. The designed rectifier was fabricated using the $0 . 1 8 \mu \mathrm { m }$ high voltage technology of a commercially available CMOS foundry. The AlN VEH with our bridge rectifier generated a DC power of $0 . 5 1 4 \mu \mathsf { W }$ at $2 . 4 9 \lor$ under an applied vibration with an acceleration amplitude of $0 . 5 \mathsf { m } / \mathsf { s } ^ { 2 }$ at a frequency of $4 6 . 6 \mathsf { H z }$ . The DC power is 1.4 times higher than that generated by the same AlN VEH with a MOSFET bridge consisting of commercially available discrete MOSFETs. $\circledcirc$ 2017 The Japan Society of Applied Physics

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Dramatic reductions in the size and power consumption of microelectronic chips are strongly driving the research and development of energy harvesting technologies.1 3) Ultralowpower electronics could conceivably run anywhere using the electricity provided by an energy harvester. Among the various types of energy harvester proposed to date, the vibration energy harvester (VEH) is the most promising because vibrations exist widely in the majority of environments. Environmental vibrations are always emitted by human activities, moving vehicles, operating machines, and various other sources. In this particular case, we focus on the vibrations emitted by pumps with outputs of around $1 0 0 \mathrm { k W }$ and develop a self-powered vibration-sensing system for the maintenance of these pumps.4,5) However, the amount of electrical power that is generated by pump vibrations is very small because the vibrations are faint, with an acceleration amplitude that is typically less than ${ \sim } 1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . Therefore, the generated power is increased on the basis of a mechanical resonance phenomenon that allows us to obtain viable levels of electrical power. A piezoelectric cantilever is preferable for this type of VEH.6 10) A cantilever VEH generates alternating current (AC) power, and thus the use of a highefficiency rectifier circuit in combination with low-power electronics is highly important because the obtainable power is very small.

In this work, we demonstrate a high-efficiency bridge rectifier that consists of four MOSFETs for an aluminum nitride (AlN) MEMS cantilever VEH. The equivalent electrical circuit of the AlN VEH, which generates a highvoltage and low-current AC output, was experimentally extracted from the dependence of the output voltage on a specific load. Using the extracted equivalent circuit, the MOSFET bridge was then simulated. The designed rectifier was subsequently fabricated by a foundry and evaluated experimentally. Using the fabricated MOSFET bridge, the AlN VEH generated a DC power of $0 . 5 1 4 \mu \mathrm { W }$ , where the DC voltage was $2 . 4 9 \mathrm { V }$ .

Fig. 1. Schematic drawing of fabrication process flow for the AlN VEH. (a) Multilayer deposition (th.: thermal). (b) Patterning. (c) Rear-side etching.

sections.heading: 2.1 Equivalent circuit of the AlN VEH
sections.text:
The equivalent circuit of the AlN VEH is extracted from the dependence of the output voltage on the load connected to the VEH. To measure this dependence, an AlN VEH was fabricated on a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer with a 10- $\mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick top Si layer and a $1 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick buried oxide (BOX) layer using a standard semiconductor MEMS process.6 22) The fabrication process flow is illustrated in Fig. 1. On the initial SOI wafer, a thermal oxide film that serves as an electrical isolation layer was formed. A $\mathrm { P t / A l N / P t }$ layer was then deposited on the oxide film by DC magnetron sputtering. The thicknesses of the Pt and AlN layers are 0.1 and $1 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , respectively. Each layer was then patterned by photolithography and reactive ion etching. The Si substrate was deeply etched from the rear side to form a thin cantilever beam and a proof mass. The fabricated VEH was then mounted on a ceramic package and electrically connected to the package by wire bonding.

![](images/b873277db129d754e8153d2480943ec683e218fea5a9860bbc39d28ff1383c8d.jpg)  
Fig. 2. AC output voltage dependence of AlN VEH on load resistance. The inset shows an equivalent electrical circuit model of the AlN VEH.

A vibration with an acceleration amplitude of $1 . 5 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ was then applied to the fabricated AlN VEH at a vibration frequency of $9 8 . 8 \mathrm { H z }$ , which is the resonant frequency of the structure. Figure 2 shows the measured AC voltage and power as a function of the load resistance. An equivalent circuit model of the AlN VEH is shown in the inset of Fig. 2. The VEH is represented electrically using a combination of an ideal current source $( I _ { \mathrm { p } } )$ , a capacitor $( C _ { \mathfrak { p } } )$ , and an internal resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { i } } )$ . The circuit parameters were then extracted by fitting of the measured voltage using the following equation of the VEH model:

$$
\dot { V } _ { \mathrm { l } } = \frac { R _ { \mathrm { i } } R _ { \mathrm { l } } } { R _ { \mathrm { i } } + R _ { \mathrm { l } } + j \omega C _ { \mathrm { p } } R _ { \mathrm { i } } R _ { \mathrm { l } } } \dot { I } _ { \mathrm { p } } .
$$

Here, $R _ { \mathrm { l } }$ is the load resistance connected to the VEH, $V _ { \mathrm { l } }$ is the voltage at the load, $j$ is the imaginary unit, and $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the VEH output. As a result, $I _ { \mathrm { p } } , C _ { \mathrm { p } } ,$ , and $R _ { \mathrm { i } }$ were determined to be $3 . 1 \mu \mathrm { A }$ , $0 . 6 6 \mathrm { n F }$ , and $4 . 1 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ respectively.

sections.heading: 2.2 MOSFET bridge rectifier
sections.text:
Figure 3 shows the schematic diagram of the rectifier used in the circuit simulations. The bridge rectifier reported in this work consists of four MOSFETs. The MOSFET gates Q2 and Q3 are connected to the positive side of the current source (I1), while the MOSFET gates Q1 and Q4 are connected to the negative side of I1. In the case where the voltage on the positive side is high, current flows from the VEH to the load through Q1 and Q4. Similarly, in the case where the voltage on the negative side is high, a current flows from the VEH to the load through Q2 and Q3. C2 is a smoothing capacitor with a capacitance of $1 \mu \mathrm { F }$ . I_veh $( I _ { \mathrm { p } } )$ C1 $( C _ { \mathfrak { p } } )$ , and R1 $( R _ { \mathrm { i } } )$ are set at $3 \mu \mathrm { A }$ , $1 \mathrm { n F }$ , and $4 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ respectively, on the basis of the circuit parameters extracted from the measurement results. A $1 \mu \mathrm { A }$ current load was connected in parallel to the smoothing capacitor.

![](images/78134aa4709845e438e572b5520efcfcd1c68b65692f654779ba40a49ed74731.jpg)  
Fig. 3. Schematic used in simulation of the MOSFET bridge rectifier with the AlN VEH.

![](images/0eef188fdc92e6907024f59a636a9d780c4e13a3d8ac7ffd265965ce099ca937.jpg)  
Fig. 4. DC output voltage dependence on device width.

The DC output voltage was simulated using the schematic depicted in Fig. 3 and also for a bridge rectifier that consisted of four Si diodes. An electrical model based on $0 . 1 8 \mu \mathrm { m }$ high-voltage technology (Silterra, Malaysia) was used. The absolute maximum rating of the gate source voltage is $\pm 1 6 \mathrm { V }$ , which is sufficient for the highest voltage generated by the piezoelectric VEH. In this technology, the device widths of both the MOSFET and the diode are variable. Figure 4 shows the simulated DC output voltages as a function of device width, and the results indicate that the MOSFET bridge is more efficient than the diode bridge. This is because the diode bridge has a voltage drop of ${ \sim } 1 . 2 \mathrm { V }$ , despite the amount of current passing through each diode. Also, Fig. 4 indicates that the output voltage of the MOSFET bridge is saturated at channel widths above ${ \sim } 1 5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ because of a trade-off between the leakage current and the on-resistance. When the channel width broadens, the onresistance simultaneously decreases. In contrast, the leakage current increases with increasing channel width.

sections.heading: 3.1 Results
sections.text:
The MOSFET bridge rectifier was fabricated using Silterra s multiproject wafer program. The features of the process technology named the CL180H32 are as follows: $0 . 1 8 \mu \mathrm { m }$ technology node, single-poly, triple gate oxide, cobalt silicide electrical contacts, and aluminum metallization with tungsten plugs. The physical design rules of an active and a poly are

![](images/2000882e505ecbf6bc86b75abfbe235540d8c29613c57a367bd488dc90f7e0a3.jpg)  
Fig. 5. (Color online) Microscopy image of fabricated MOSFET bridge rectifier die.

![](images/06a8fdc9d2447d7980ec8bfe4772c483146e40d73e6b49908f8867c36b4bb59b.jpg)  
Fig. 6. (Color online) (a) Measured AC output voltage of AlN VEH. (b) Measured output voltage across MOSFET rectifier.

6.7 and $6 . 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , respectively. Figure 5 shows a microscopy image of the fabricated die. The channel width is $2 5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and the die dimensions are $0 . 5 \times 0 . 8 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ . The fabricated rectifier was assembled in a quad flat no-leads (QFN) package with a size of $1 . 5 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ .

The output voltage of the AlN VEH was measured under an applied vibration with an acceleration amplitude of 0.5 $\mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ at a frequency of $4 6 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ using an oscilloscope (OSC) with an input impedance of $1 0 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ . Figure 6(a) shows that the VEH generates a sinusoidal AC voltage with an amplitude of $3 . 2 \mathrm { V }$ . The output voltage across the rectifier is depicted in Fig. 6(b). The maximum rectified output voltage is $2 . 7 \mathrm { V }$ , which indicates that the voltage drop at the rectifier is $0 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ . This means that the MOSFET bridge rectifier demonstrates a higher efficiency than a diode bridge because the voltage drop of the diode bridge is ${ \sim } 1 . 2 \mathrm { V }$ .

The DC output voltage generated by the AlN VEH was then measured using the measurement setup shown in Fig. 7(a). The fabricated VEH was mounted on a ceramic package and electrically connected by Au wire bonding.

![](images/ebc252cfe1aee23926aa9d7ca57fcf07094fdd4a30ddbb7096b1a4f7715441a7.jpg)  
Fig. 7. (Color online) (a) Measurement setup (ext. vib.: external vibration, acc.: acceleration). (b) Measured DC output voltage. (c) Measured DC output power.

The VEH, the rectifier in the QFN package, and the load resistance were connected using cables. The load resistance was varied over a range from 1 to $2 0 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ , which includes the internal impedance $( R _ { \mathrm { i } } )$ of the AlN VEH $( { \sim } 4 \mathrm { M } \Omega )$ . Therefore, a digital multimeter with a high input impedance of ${ > } 1 0 \mathrm { G } \Omega$ was used to measure the output voltage. A vibration with an acceleration amplitude of $0 . 5 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ was applied to the VEH while the vibration frequency was varied over the range from 45.5 to $4 7 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ , including the resonant frequency. The vibration acceleration was maintained at $0 . 5 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ in this frequency range by proportional-integral control. Figures 7(b) and 7(c) show the DC voltage and power, respectively. The maximum power of $0 . 5 1 4 \mu \mathrm { W }$ was obtained for a load resistance of $1 2 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ and a vibration frequency of $4 6 . 6 \mathrm { H z }$ . The voltage at this maximum power was $2 . 4 9 \mathrm { V }$ .

sections.heading: 3.2 Benchmark
sections.text: Using a bridge rectifier composed of commercially available MOSFETs (Toshiba SSM3K116TU), we measured the DC output voltage of the AlN VEH under the same measurement conditions, as shown in Figs. 8(a) and 8(b). The MOSFET has an absolute maximum gate source voltage rating of $\pm 1 2 \mathrm { V }$ , which is sufficiently high for the piezoelectric VEH. As a result of these measurements, a maximum power of $0 . 3 7 2 \mu \mathrm { W }$ was obtained at a load resistance of 5 MΩ with a vibration frequency of $4 6 . 6 \mathrm { H z }$ . The efficiency of the proposed bridge rectifier is ${ \sim } 1 . 4$ times higher than that of the SSM3K116TU bridge. Note that the SSM3K116TU is not intended for rectifier applications. The load resistance (5 MΩ) at maximum power when the SSM3K116TU bridge was used differs from that (12 MΩ) at maximum power when the proposed MOSFET bridge was used. This is probably because the SSM3K116TU has a higher reverse leakage current than the MOSFET used in the proposed bridge.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text: In this work, we demonstrate a high-efficiency MOSFET bridge rectifier for use with an AlN piezoelectric MEMS cantilever VEH. The MOSFET bridge was specifically designed for use with a high-voltage and low-current AlN VEH. The MOSFET bridge was fabricated using the Silterra $0 . 1 8 \mu \mathrm { m }$ high-voltage technology and subsequently evaluated. The AlN VEH with the proposed MOSFET bridge generated an electrical power of $0 . 5 1 4 \mu \mathrm { W }$ at $2 . 4 9 \mathrm { V }$ from a vibration with an acceleration amplitude of $0 . 5 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ at a frequency of $4 6 . 6 \mathrm { H z }$ , which is comparable to the actual pump vibration. This output power would be able to drive a small-scale analog electrical circuit, e.g., the power management circuit that we use for a self-powered wireless vibrationsensing system.5) We therefore believe that our proposed MOSFET bridge will be helpful in the realization of an Internet-of-Things (IoT)-based society.
